pl-l4d32c2-d1e115.summary: States that the testimonies below prove that a husband cannot keep continence without his wife's consent.

pl-l4d32c2-d1e118.summary: Quotes Augustine: if a husband says 'I want to be continent' and the wife does not, he cannot; should your continence make her a fornicator? If she marries another while you live, she is an adulteress; God does not want such loss for such gain. Render the debt; even if you do not demand it, render it; God will count it as perfect sanctification if you render what you owe rather than demand what is owed.
claims: A husband may not be continent against his wife's will.
Rendering the debt is counted as holiness.

pl-l4d32c2-d1e127.summary: Adds Augustine: if your husband had wanted continence and you did not, he would be bound to render the debt, and God would count it as continence if he yielded to your weakness; whoever, compassionate toward the wife's weakness, renders without demanding, or marries for his own weakness, grieving that he could not be without a wife, awaits the last day securely.
claims: Yielding to the spouse's weakness is counted as continence.

pl-l4d32c2-d1e137.summary: Adds Augustine: one cause alone would make us forbid fulfilling your vow: if your spouse refused to undertake it through weakness of mind or flesh; such vows must not be made by spouses except by common consent and will; if made rashly, the rashness is to be corrected rather than the promise paid, since God does not demand what one vowed of another's property but forbids usurping it.
claims: Spouses vow continence only by common consent.
A rash vow of another's right is not to be kept.

pl-l4d32c2-d1e143.summary: Adds Augustine: the Apostle allowed spouses to deprive each other of the debt, even for a time to pray, only by consent.
claims: Abstaining even for prayer requires consent.

pl-l4d32c2-d1e152.summary: Adds Augustine: the Law clearly placed the wife under the husband so that her vows of abstinence are not fulfilled unless he permits; if he first permits and later forbids, the sin is his, yet the Law did not tell her to disregard his later prohibition.
claims: Under the Law a wife's vows needed her husband's permission.

pl-l4d32c2-d1e158.summary: Concludes that neither husband nor wife can offer continence to God without common assent, nor should one deny the other the debt.

pl-l4d32c2-d1e161.summary: Asks whether one who has released the other from his right can recall the other to the former service, as Augustine seemed to suggest.

pl-l4d32c2-d1e167.summary: Reports that some think a wife who, with her husband's permission, promised continence without leaving his house cannot fulfil it if he forbids, because of his dignity as head; but it is better understood of a case where he grants her to vow and forbids before the vow; if she has changed her habit, she cannot be recalled, since one who allowed his wife to be veiled may not take another but must also convert.
claims: A husband may forbid a vow before it is made.
A wife who has taken the habit cannot be recalled.

pl-l4d32c2.summary: Proves that a husband cannot keep continence without his wife's consent: Augustine says his continence must not make her a fornicator, and God will count it as holiness if he renders what he owes; vows of continence are not to be made by spouses except by common consent, and a rash vow is to be corrected rather than fulfilled, since God does not accept a vow of another's goods; even for prayer the Apostle allows abstaining only by consent; under the Law a wife's vows of abstinence required her husband's permission. So neither may offer continence to God without the other or deny the debt. Whether one who released the other can recall the right: Lombard holds that a husband may forbid a wife's vow before it is made, but if she has taken the habit she cannot be recalled.
claims: Neither spouse may vow continence without the other's consent.
A rash vow of continence by one spouse is to be corrected, not fulfilled.
A spouse who has taken the religious habit with permission cannot be recalled.
